item.title: Dozens killed in two mass shootings in South Africa
item.description:
Two mass shootings carried out roughly four hours apart left at least 27 people dead in South Africa over the weekend, pushing the death toll from township massacres this week to at least 38. The deadlier attack began around 9:30 p.m. Saturday in Wedela, a township in Gauteng province’s West Rand mining district. Police said eight men carrying AK-47s and handguns fired on patrons drinking outside a tavern, then went inside and kept shooting. Seventeen people — 13 men and four women — were killed and 15 others were wounded. The gunmen took cellphones from some victims before leaving in two vehicles. item.title: Northern Ireland protesters block Orange Order march into Catholic area
item.description:
Tensions are running high in Northern Ireland after the High Court in Belfast approved a controversial parade. Around 2,000 protesters have blocked the route into a Catholic area where the Protestant march was due to pass. It is the first time in nearly 30 years that the Orange Order has been allowed to march along this route, which was a notorious flashpoint before the 1998 Good Friday Agreement largely brought an end to the bloodshed of the Troubles. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has appealed for calm on all sides, saying he does not want to see Northern Ireland “go backwards.”

item.title: Why Germany is building an ark for US climate data
item.description:
In a modern five-story building in the center of Hamburg, Germany, technicians are preparing to install several new “racks” — gray metal casings that hold computing hardware — alongside the scores that already line the narrow, dimly lit corridors of the German Climate Computing Center, or DKRZ, one of the world’s largest repositories for climate simulation data. The new equipment will add about 5 petabytes of storage capacity to the 254 petabytes of data already stored here. One petabyte of data is equivalent to the storage space needed for roughly 200 million high-resolution images. Under normal circumstances, the DKRZ’s mission is to provide computing power and storage to the German climate science community. But these new racks will serve a different and highly sensitive purpose: They will store backup versions of climate simulations from the other side of the Atlantic. The operation…

item.title: True Crime Reports: The Dosa King’s Deadly Obsession
item.description:
Before she became infamous as one of the youngest American women ever sentenced to die, Christa Gail Pike was a North Carolina teenager who broke into a community center to steal some candy. At 5-foot-3, with thick auburn curls, she’d been in trouble at home and in school but not with the law. A juvenile court judge put Pike on probation, but she ran afoul of the rules. In the fall of 1991, when she was 15, Pike was sent to the Juvenile Evaluation Center in Swannanoa. She arrived just before Thanksgiving. Nestled in the Blue Ridge mountains, just minutes away from Asheville, the center first opened in the 1960s as a “haven for troubled children,” in the words of the press. It was supposed to be an alternative to more severe “training schools,” but by the 1990s was skewed toward punishment.
